name: DIRTY ROTTEN TENDRILS BURGER (comes with pea tendrils, not rotten)

recipe.history:
Pea tendrils — the curling, delicate shoots and leaves that emerge from the tips of growing pea plants — have been harvested and eaten in China for over a thousand years. In Cantonese cuisine, dòu miáo (豆苗) are a beloved vegetable, stir-fried with garlic and sesame oil or blanched and served simply dressed. The tendril's flavor carries the pure, grassy sweetness of fresh peas without any starchiness, a concentrated expression of the spring garden. In northern China and across Southeast Asia, farmers learned long ago that trimming these growing tips not only provided a nutritious food source but also encouraged the plant to put more energy into pod production. The practice spread through Chinese diaspora communities around the world, and pea tendrils became emblematic of early spring eating throughout East and Southeast Asia.

Pea shoots and tendrils arrived in American culinary consciousness in earnest during the farm-to-table movement of the 1990s and early 2000s. Chefs in San Francisco's Chinatown had been using them for decades, but it was the broader embrace of local, seasonal produce that brought them to tasting menus and farmers market stalls across the country. Their bright flavor, wispy texture, and striking visual appeal made them an instant favorite as a burger topping in the hands of inventive American cooks. Unlike heavier greens, pea tendrils wilt just slightly under the heat of a resting patty, taking on a silky quality while retaining their verdant snap and sweetness. They replaced the tired iceberg lettuce on forward-thinking burger menus with something alive and seasonal.

The first pea tendrils I ever put on a burger were an accident — I had bought a large bag at the farmers market, used half in a stir-fry the night before, and had the rest sitting in the fridge the next morning when the lunch burger craving hit. I had nothing else green in the house. I piled them on out of necessity and stood at the counter eating one of the best burgers I had made in years. The tendrils caught the juices from the patty and wilted into something almost saucy, their pea sweetness threading through the beefy, salty crust. I have never gone back to plain lettuce since that afternoon.

Medium rare — 130 to 135°F at the center of the patty — is the only temperature at which a burger achieves its full potential. The beef's natural sugars and amino acids have undergone the Maillard reaction on the exterior, building a crust of staggering complexity, while the interior remains flushed pink and tender, the fat distributed in glistening pockets throughout every bite. Pea tendrils, being delicate, need a warm but not scorching surface to rest on; they drape perfectly over a medium-rare patty just off the heat, wilting gently without going limp or losing their color. A well-done patty would be too dry and hot, turning the tendrils into sad, gray strings. Cooking to medium rare is not recklessness — it is precision, care, and the understanding that beef at its best is alive with flavor and moisture.
ingredients: 1/3 cup mashed potato (from 1 medium Yukon Gold), cooled
4 oz fresh pea tendrils (pea shoots), cleaned and trimmed
Salt and white pepper to taste
instructions: 1. Make the potato rolls: Boil one medium Yukon Gold potato, peel and rice or mash until completely smooth, no lumps. Measure 1/3 cup; cool to room temperature.
2. Dissolve yeast in warm water with sugar; bloom 10 minutes until foamy.

3. In a stand mixer with the dough hook, combine flour and salt. Add yeast mixture, warm milk, mashed potato, butter, and egg. Mix on low 3 minutes to incorporate, then medium for 7–8 minutes until the dough is smooth, supple, and slightly tacky.
4. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise at room temperature 1–1.5 hours until doubled.
5. Punch down dough and divide into 4 equal pieces (about 130g each). Shape into smooth rounds; place on parchment-lined baking sheet 3 inches apart. Cover and proof 45–60 minutes until puffy.
6. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush rolls with egg wash. Bake 17–20 minutes until golden. Cool on rack.

7. Make the garlic lemon aioli: Combine mayonnaise, minced garlic, lemon juice, lemon zest, and Dijon. Season with salt and white pepper. Whisk smooth. Refrigerate at least 20 minutes to let garlic mellow.

8. Dress the pea tendrils just before assembling: In a large bowl, gently toss pea tendrils with olive oil, lemon juice, flaky salt, and black pepper. Do not overdress — the tendrils should be lightly coated, not wet.

9. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into 3/4-inch-thick patties slightly wider than the buns. Press a dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and onion powder.
10. Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until very hot. Add oil and swirl.
11. Place patties in the pan. Cook undisturbed 3–4 minutes until a deep, even crust forms on the bottom.

12. Flip patties once. Lay fontina slices over each patty. Cook 2–3 more minutes, tenting with foil if needed to melt the cheese, until an instant-read thermometer reads 130–135°F (54–57°C) in the center. Remove to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.
13. Split buns and toast cut-side down in the skillet fat 60–90 seconds until golden.
14. Assemble: Spread garlic lemon aioli on both cut faces of each bun. Place a tomato slice and red onion ring on the bottom bun; season tomato with flaky salt.
15. Set the cheese-covered patty on top. Pile a generous mound of dressed pea tendrils over the patty, letting the tendrils cascade over the sides.
16. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately while the tendrils are fresh and just barely beginning to wilt from the patty's warmth.
